reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs at 23 with a 12.2% walk rate and a 92.9 mph average exit velocity is a profile that doesn't need much defending. The Statcast contact quality, a .369 xwOBA and 50.5% hard-hit rate, lines up neatly with what the projection asks him to do at full health across 700 plate appearances, a .280/.362/.542 slash that puts him squarely in the MVP conversation for a rebuilding Tampa Bay club. His strikeout rate is a comfortable 18.2%, well below where you'd start worrying for a power hitter, and the walk rate says the zone control is already mature for his age. The one honest drag is in the field: a 1st-percentile OAA suggests the defensive profile is a real liability, so everything hinges on whether he stays at third or gets pushed to a corner where the bat has to carry even more weight.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-whiff tension here is worth sitting with: a 21.5% barrel rate and 95.2 mph average exit velocity that both grade at the ceiling, paired with a 31.3% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league. What resolves it is the walk rate. At 16.8% he's drawing enough free passes to carry an approach that swings and misses plenty, and the .424 xwOBA says the damage when he does connect is severe enough that pitchers have no clean way to attack him. The whole profile hinges on whether that chase rate, a disciplined 22.3%, holds as he ages into his prime; if pitchers draw him out of the zone more consistently, the strikeouts get uglier and the walks dry up together, but if the discipline holds, the projection's .918 OPS across 748 plate appearances is a conservative translation of what Statcast already sees.

The Statcast shape is a little unusual: elite contact quality sitting well above what the xBA of .254 would suggest, which means the hit tool is lagging behind the power tool, and that 34.2% chase rate is the reason. reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .411 xwOBA and a 2.72 xERA on the same player card is not a normal document. The bat profile is almost entirely elite, contact quality clustering at the 96th-to-98th percentile range, and a 14.0% walk rate that keeps the .391 OBP honest even with a 22.8% strikeout rate that sits squarely league-average. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball paired with 30.4% whiff rate does real damage, and the 3.8% barrel rate against him explains why the xERA lands at 2.72. The projection carries both roles forward: 38 home runs and a .935 OPS as a hitter, full rotation value as a pitcher, and the whole thing hinges on whether he stays healthy enough to accumulate in both directions across 696 plate appearances. If he does, there is no comparable player to anchor this against.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 40.6 K% that sits at the literal ceiling of the Statcast era is the headline, but the xERA of 1.97 is what makes this a serious profile, not a strikeout-rate novelty act. The 2625 rpm spin on a 100.6 mph fastball explains the 38.5% whiff rate, and a barrel rate of 3.0% tells you the stuff isn't just missing bats by luck — when contact happens, it's soft. The walk rate at 6.1% is the one lever: if it creeps up as lineups get deeper looks, the xwOBA of .218 gets harder to sustain at rotation volume, but right now the projection of a 2.10 ERA over 181.8 innings reads as a true ace, not a relief arm running a hot stretch.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .470 with an 11.3% barrel rate, and the projection extends that into 36 home runs with a .524 SLG — the distance between those two numbers is speed doing real work. Abrams runs 28.5 ft/s, good enough to project 29 steals on top of the power, and his .352 xwOBA says the underlying contact quality earns most of what the slash line claims. The one genuine crack in the profile is a 36.7% chase rate, which puts him in the bottom fifth of the league on that metric and keeps the ceiling from being higher. If pitchers consistently exploit it, the strikeout rate climbs off its current middling 21.6% and the walk rate, already sitting right at league average, compresses further; if it stabilizes even modestly, you're looking at a shortstop projecting .280/.351/.524 with 36 home runs and 29 steals, which is a genuine first-division player.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The 94.3 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, and the rest of his contact profile, 15.1% barrels and 52.9% hard-hit rate, confirms that when De La Cruz connects, he hits the ball as hard as almost anyone alive. The profile hinges entirely on the strikeout rate: 27.6% K% undercuts what a .366 xwOBA says he should be producing, and if he can't find two or three more contact points, the power plays intermittently rather than consistently. The projection, .269/.346/.484 with 28 home runs and 31 stolen bases across a full 639 PA, is what the skill set earns when the bat-to-ball rate holds at its current ceiling rather than sliding further; it falls apart if the whiff rate climbs and pitchers find a lane to exploit. He's a true middle-of-the-order shortstop if the strikeout stabilizes, a volatile power-speed lottery ticket if it doesn't.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact quality and the chase rate are pulling in opposite directions, and that tension defines the Walker profile. His 93.2 mph average exit velocity sits at the 97th percentile, and a 13.7% barrel rate backs it up: when he connects, the damage is legitimate. The problem is a 35.1% chase rate and 30.7% whiff rate that bleed strikeouts, keeping a .281 xBA from fully showing up in the box score and capping what the raw power could produce. If he ever tightens the zone, a .495 xSLG profile at 24 years old becomes something imposing; if the swing decisions stay where they are, he's a .273/.336/.479 masher with 31 home runs and real stolen-base value, a very good player who left something on the table.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The 18.2% barrel rate and 57.4% hard-hit rate sit at the center of a profile that is otherwise genuinely uncomfortable to look at. Kurtz strikes out 32.2% of the time and whiffs on 36.5% of pitches he swings at, but he chases just 23.0% of offerings outside the zone, and that discipline is what keeps the walk rate at 18.1% and the whole thing from caving. The .375 xwOBA reflects a hitter whose damage on contact is severe enough that pitchers can't simply avoid the zone; the .245 xBA reflects what happens when 36.5% of his swings miss. If the strikeout rate creeps higher as pitchers probe the whiff vulnerability, you're left with a boom-or-bust first baseman whose walks buy him lineup spots but not a full-time role; if it holds where it is, the projection's .499 slugging and 34 home runs describe a middle-of-the-order piece who earns his at-bats the hard way.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a cautionary tale about how good defense and a crowded counting-stat line can obscure a hitter who is quietly in trouble. His xwOBA sits at .303, well below a league-average mark, and his xBA of .234 and xSLG of .383 both land in the bottom third of qualified hitters. The 44.3% hard-hit rate is genuine contact quality, but the barrel rate of 7.2% and a chase rate of 31.8% explain why it doesn't convert — he's hitting the ball hard to the wrong places often enough that the expected numbers bleed downward. The projection's .231/.305/.413 line with 27 home runs across 726 PA is basically what that Statcast card says he is: a shortstop with enough raw power to be interesting and enough plate-discipline drag to keep him from being more than a second-division regular at the position unless the chase rate tightens.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .422 xwOBA tells you almost everything: Soto is making elite contact quality, chasing only 19.8% of pitches while walking at 17.5%, and the combination produces an expected profile that the .948 OPS projection roughly tracks. What separates him isn't raw thump, because the exit velocity and barrel rate are excellent but not historically freakish, but that the discipline forces pitchers into the zone where his .589 xSLG lives. The projection at 29 home runs and a .411 OBP across 510 PA is conservative relative to what the Statcast profile suggests he's capable of, so the sprint speed and fielding sitting at the bottom of the percentile card are the real cost-benefit item: you're paying for a bat that earns it, carrying a corner profile that has to keep producing at this contact level to justify the contract.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact-plus-patience combination here is the argument. Across AAA, A+, and A this year, Jenkins is hitting .294/.398/.482 with 32 walks against 33 strikeouts in 231 plate appearances, and when you translate that discipline to the big-league level it sketches a K% around 18.6 against a league that whiffs at 22.0, with a walk rate that clears the MLB average by more than two points. The ISO translates to .146, which sits right at the MLB mean, so the profile isn't carrying a power story — it's carrying a hit-tool-and-zone-management story, and that's a profile that works as long as the contact rates hold when velocity stiffens. If they do, Jenkins grows into an everyday center fielder; if the strikeout number climbs toward league average at the highest level, you're looking at a second-division regular who still gets on base.

reports.name: Hagen Smith
reports.published_report: The 13.5 K/9 at AAA is the loudest number in the profile, and it translates to 10.3 per nine against MLB hitters while the league sits at 8.6. The problem sitting right next to it is 39 walks across 56 innings, a 6.3 BB/9 that becomes 5.0 in translation when the MLB average is 3.2. Those two facts together explain why the K-BB% lands at only 18% despite elite strikeout volume. If the command firms up, this is a back-end starter with a legitimate weapon; if it doesn't, he's a depth arm whose swing-and-miss can't outrun the free passes.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is genuinely loud where it matters most: a .289 xBA ranks in the 94th percentile, and a .503 xSLG suggests the projection's .520 slugging isn't borrowed time. What makes the profile fragile is sitting right alongside those numbers, a 40.2% chase rate that puts him in the bottom 5% of the league, paired with a 4.4% walk rate that's nearly as bad. He makes enough contact at 16.0% strikeouts to survive the aggression, and pitchers who get ahead of him early have to actually put the ball somewhere he can't do damage, because when he connects at 91.4 mph average exit velo he hits it hard. If the chase rate ever gets exploited at scale, the walk rate offers no floor, and this entire profile runs through contact quality holding up against an opponent that keeps feeding him pitches outside the zone.

reports.name: Tarik Skubal
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the anchor of everything here: 3.7% BB rate ranks at the 100th percentile, meaning he's essentially the best in baseball at not giving hitters a free pass, and that control is what props a 2.99 xERA and a .269 xwOBA into genuinely elite territory rather than good-on-paper numbers. The 36.5% chase rate and 31.0% strikeout rate confirm the shape — batters expand for him because they have to, because he isn't expanding for them first. Barrel rate sits at 7.5%, ordinary enough that contact management isn't his calling card, but the projection's 2.78 ERA over 162.6 innings is built on a pitcher who earns outs before hitters ever get to square one. The whole profile hinges on that command holding; if the walk rate creeps up, the rest of the structure softens fast.

reports.name: Luis Lara
reports.published_report: The contact and patience are loud: a .432 OBP at AAA, 54 walks against 48 strikeouts in 346 plate appearances, and a K% that translates to 17.6% at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer strikes out at 22.0%. Lara hits for average and gets on base at an elite clip, and the 24 stolen bases give him a real center-field offensive profile. The translation is honest about what he isn't, though: a .130 MLB-equivalent ISO tells you the game-to-game impact depends on contact and speed, not power, and if the BABIP softens when he faces better pitching, the ceiling lands closer to a low-end everyday regular than anything beyond it. That's the profile — a CF who earns his at-bats with a strike-zone approach that would play up immediately, but whose ceiling is ultimately capped by what the bat does when contact rates normalize.

reports.name: Luis Arraez

The catch is that a .305 xwOBA and a Hard-Hit% of 20.3 tell you there's almost no over-the-fence threat here, so everything runs through that batting average holding — if the BABIP environment turns hostile against an 86.9 mph exit velo profile, what's left is a slap hitter with a 5.5% walk rate that won't carry him. What makes Paredes work is the walk rate, 9.4% BB% keeping the on-base number alive even when the exit velocity isn't doing him any favors. reports.name: Gavin Williams
reports.published_report: The strikeout profile is elite and the contact profile is a problem, and that tension is basically the whole read on Gavin Williams. A 31.6% K rate sits at the 95th percentile, the 30.9% whiff rate backs it up, and yet hitters who do make contact are barreling him up at 11.5% with a 49.2% hard-hit rate that lands at the 2nd percentile for pitchers — meaning almost no one in the league gives up harder contact when they miss. The xERA sits at 4.00 while the projection calls for a 3.72 ERA across 192.4 innings, so the gap closes only if he limits the damage when contact happens, probably through sequencing or strand rate that the underlying contact numbers don't guarantee. If he holds that K rate and tightens the barrel suppression even modestly, he profiles as a true mid-rotation anchor; if the hard contact keeps finding gaps, the strikeouts become expensive decoration on a 4-plus ERA arm.

reports.name: Cade Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest number in this profile, and it earns that volume. Smith is punching out 34.7% of batters faced with a 34.2% whiff rate, both sitting in the 96th-97th percentile range, and that combination reflects a genuine swing-and-miss arsenal rather than a contact-management story. The hard contact numbers are less comfortable, a 44.3% hard-hit rate and average exit velocity of 91.8 mph grading near the bottom of the league, but the strikeout volume has been outrunning the damage badly enough that his xwOBA sits at .283 and xERA at 3.32. The projection has him as a closer, 41 saves and a 2.65 ERA over 72.9 innings, and that holds if the strikeout rate stays where it is; if it regresses toward what the barrel and exit-velo numbers hint is lurking underneath, the gap between the ERA and the hard contact closes fast.

reports.name: Josue De Paula
reports.published_report: The contact and the plate discipline are both loud, and at 21 in Double-A that combination almost never shows up this clean. Josue De Paula is hitting .309 with a 14% walk rate and a matching 14% strikeout rate across 430 PA at AA, and the translation says those rates don't evaporate at the big-league level — an 18% K rate when MLB hitters are striking out at 22%, a walk rate that edges above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The power is the open question: a .214 ISO at AA translates to .159, right around the MLB average, which puts this profile in disciplined-contact territory more than true impact bat. If the power firms up as he fills out, he's an everyday right fielder; if it plateaus here, he's a high-OBP regular who earns his roster spot with the bat-to-ball and the 27 stolen bases rather than the extra bases.

reports.name: Bryan Woo
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the spine of this profile: Woo's 5.1% BB% sits at the 94th percentile, and that control is what props up everything else in a band that otherwise runs 58-to-69th percentile. His 34.7% chase rate is excellent, but the 24.6% whiff rate is modest, meaning he induces bad swings on pitches outside the zone more than he blows hitters away. The xERA of 3.52 is the honest signal; his ability to limit free passes keeps him from paying for a 43.1% hard-hit rate that ranks in the bottom fifth of starters. If the control erodes, the whole profile thins fast, because there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, but if it holds, 169.2 projected innings at a 4.13 ERA looks like a quiet, durable mid-rotation starter doing exactly what he is.

reports.name: Drew Rasmussen
reports.published_report: The 4.3% walk rate is the skeleton of this profile, sitting at the 98th percentile and explaining almost everything downstream. Rasmussen doesn't miss enough bats to be a strikeout-first arm, because 24.8% whiff rate is right at the middle of the league, but a 34.0% chase rate and that elite control mean hitters are almost never getting on base for free, which is how you arrive at a 3.13 xERA and a .275 xwOBA against. The projection, 3.27 ERA over 170.5 innings, asks him to stay healthy for a full season, and that's the real hinge: a contact-management profile with his level of stuff has no margin for a prolonged IL stint, because there's no swing-and-miss floor to fall back on if he's diminished. When he's right, he's a legitimate mid-rotation starter who earns his innings; when he's not, the 2518 rpm spin and the control won't be enough on their own.

reports.name: Geraldo Perdomo
reports.published_report: A 15.0% walk rate paired with a 12.3% strikeout rate is a profile most big leaguers can't approach, and it's the engine behind everything here. Perdomo doesn't hit the ball hard, 87.1 mph average exit velocity and a 3.1% barrel rate are both in the bottom tenth of the league, so the .325 xwOBA sitting at the 58th percentile is almost entirely a walk and contact-avoidance story rather than a power story. The projection's .356 OBP reflects that reality: he gets on base at a rate well above a typical shortstop, steals 26 bags, scores 82 runs, and provides elite defense at a premium position, but the .368 SLG makes clear he's not carrying an offense. If the contact quality stays suppressed and the strikeout rate creeps up even modestly, the OBP advantage shrinks fast and what's left is a light-hitting shortstop who runs a little.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact-and-plate-discipline profile is genuinely ugly, but the ball-striking underneath it is real enough to argue for patience. A 55.7% hard-hit rate sits at the 98th percentile, average exit velocity of 93.1 mph checks in at the 95th, and a 14.6% barrel rate lands at the 93rd — that's a legitimate power core, not a guy running hot on a thin sample. The problem is a 36.9% chase rate and a 28.2% strikeout rate that both sit in the bottom fifth of the league, which is why a .347 xwOBA and .482 xSLG haven't yet translated into a line worth celebrating, and why the projection lands at .252/.312/.449. If he tightens his zone coverage even modestly, 25 home runs in 584 projected plate appearances is probably a floor; if the chase rate stays where it is, he's a well-below-average OBP guy living and dying by the long ball, plus a 6th-percentile fielding profile that limits his margin for error.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA of .300 is the loudest number in this profile, and it creates an immediate puzzle: how does a hitter with 88.3 mph average exit velocity and a 5.6% barrel rate produce batted-ball expectations that good? The answer is contact quality of a different shape, hitting the ball where it's supposed to go, consistently, rather than hitting it hard. That 99th-percentile xBA sits alongside a 28.4% whiff rate and a 35.0% chase rate that both grade well below average, so the floor here depends entirely on whether his bat-to-ball skills stay sharp against pitchers who've now had a full look at him. If they do, the projection's .292/.347/.468 is honest, probably a touch conservative given the underlying contact profile; if his chase rate climbs and pitchers start exploiting his zone decisions, the power ceiling never grows loud to begin with and you're left with a quick, 29.2 ft/s shortstop who hits singles.

The problem is the whiff rate, a 32.9% figure sitting at the 10th percentile, which is what keeps the xBA at .246 and caps the projection at .252 AVG across roughly 394 plate appearances. He's a catcher who can hurt you badly on the pitches he gets to; the whole profile hinges on whether he tightens contact enough to stop pitchers from simply working him off the plate and waiting. If the swing-and-miss stays where it is, you've got a slugging catcher with a .772 OPS ceiling, useful but short of impact; if he buys back even a few whiff points, the 82nd-percentile xSLG starts showing up in the actual slash line and he becomes something harder to game plan around.

reports.published_report: The contact is the story here: a 12% strikeout rate across A+ & A at 18 years old, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 18.2% while the league sits at 22.0% — most 18-year-olds aren't making this kind of contact anywhere near this level. Juneiker Caceres is hitting .314/.407/.525 across 280 plate appearances with 34 walks against only 33 strikeouts, a balance that most hitters never achieve at any age. The power translation is the open question: his .212 ISO in the minors softens to a .138 MLB equivalent, and the league average is .150, meaning if the raw power doesn't carry forward, the ceiling compresses fast from a low-end everyday right fielder to a bench bat who reaches base at a nice clip. reports.name: Jared Jones
reports.published_report: The fastball at 98.4 mph with 2546 rpm spin is a genuine weapon, and the 30.9% whiff rate shows hitters aren't solving it in-zone. Jones's 27.9 K% and xERA of 3.03 say the underlying profile is sharper than most of what Pittsburgh is rolling out, and the .271 xwOBA against backs that up. The one tension in the profile is chase rate: at 29.2%, he's not getting many weak swings outside the zone, so the whole strikeout operation runs through hitters failing to square up his stuff in the zone rather than chasing — which works until a better lineup makes him pay for the 7.2 BB%. The projection's 3.73 ERA and 101 innings reflect some health discount, and if he stays in the rotation and the walk rate holds, you're looking at a genuine mid-rotation arm for Pittsburgh.

reports.name: Willson Contreras
reports.published_report: A .387 xwOBA at the 97th percentile is a legitimate top-of-the-lineup offensive profile, and it's sitting in a catcher's body. The xSLG of .508 and a 14.3% barrel rate explain how he generates that — this isn't contact volume inflating the number, it's impact. The wrinkle is a 31.0% whiff rate and 33.9% chase rate that both land in the bottom quarter of the league, meaning pitchers who can make him expand will, and they do. If he's hitting .274/.377/.512 in Boston at age 34 while catching, he's one of the five or six most valuable offensive catchers in baseball; if the swing-and-miss escalates as he ages, you're left with a guy who still has real power but stops making pitchers pay for mistakes the way that .387 xwOBA says he currently does.

reports.name: Coby Mayo

The projection lands at .212/.282/.424 over 394 plate appearances, which reads like the math working exactly as advertised: genuine over-the-fence power in the .424 SLG, a floor that's essentially an all-or-nothing bat. If the whiff rate bends even modestly toward league-average territory, a second-division everyday corner emerges; if it doesn't, what remains is a platoon piece who slugs his way to roster relevance.

reports.name: Evan Carter
reports.published_report: The chase rate tells you almost everything you need to know about what Carter can be: 19.6% is elite, and it's why his 13.0% walk rate is among the best in this Rangers lineup. The problem is that the contact quality doesn't back the discipline up — an .207 xBA and 38.2% hard-hit rate suggest a hitter who lays off good pitches and then doesn't punish the ones he swings at. The projection (.321 OBP, .364 SLG across 457 PA) lands him as a second-division regular whose value leans on getting on base and the 20 projected steals, and that's a real profile if the strikeout rate stays manageable. Everything hinges on whether the bat-to-ball improves enough at 23 to turn that walk rate into genuine on-base value rather than a floor that papers over weak contact.

Seventeen home runs across 350 AAA plate appearances in 2026, with a .247 ISO that translates to .181 at the MLB level, which already clears the league average mark by a meaningful margin, and for a 24-year-old first baseman, that's the one thing the profile has going for it that doesn't require squinting.

The tension is that everything else trails. His .234 average at AAA comes with a .244 BABIP, meaning he's not being unlucky into that number, and his .340 OBP depends entirely on 41 walks holding up against better pitching. The translated strikeout rate, 21.1% against a 22.0% MLB average, is actually fine, but the contact quality underneath the ISO has to carry a profile this thin on hit-tool upside. If the power translates and the walk rate holds, he's a useful bench piece; if the .244 BABIP is telling you what the average will do in a tougher environment, what's left is a slugging percentage propped up by the long ball at a position with no margin for error.

report_llm.text: The .431 OBP at AAA is the whole argument, and it's also the problem. Brett Bateman has posted a .388 BABIP across 332 plate appearances this season, and everything downstream, the .311 average, the 97th-percentile on-base rate, lives inside that number. Strip the BABIP to something earthbound and the .431 collapses, because the translated ISO of .114 sits well short of the MLB average .150 and the power hasn't shown any inclination to close that gap. What he does own is discipline and legs: 58 walks against 61 strikeouts translates to a 13.2% walk rate at the MLB level, well above the 8.5% average, and 20 stolen bases give him a speed dimension that survives a BABIP correction. If the contact quality holds even partly, he's a useful bench piece in center; if the BABIP regresses hard, the bat thins into organizational depth with a good eye.

The plate discipline translates to a 14.2% walk rate against major-league hitters at a level where the strikeout rate also plays, sitting below the MLB mean at 19.3%. The power is limited: a .157 ISO at A+ softens to .12 in translation, which is below average, and six home runs in 431 trips confirm the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat rather than an everyday impact piece. Forty-eight stolen bases give the profile a second gear, and if he maintains the walk rate as he climbs, he's a useful, on-base-heavy piece; if pitchers above A+ start exploiting the power gap, the floor is depth.

At AAA in 2026, Spencer Jones is posting a .284 ISO across 233 plate appearances, which renders to .192 against MLB pitching, real power, but paired with a strikeout rate that translates to 28.1% when the AAA average sits at 22.0%. The discipline is genuinely there, 31 walks against 72 strikeouts at AAA, and the 10.5% translated walk rate clears its MLB counterpart of 8.5%, so the question isn't whether he can take a pitch. It's whether the strikeout rate compresses enough at the highest level to let the power carry a lineup spot, and if it doesn't, the .358 BABIP propping that .273 average comes down and you're left with a bench bat who swings and misses too much to start every day.

reports.name: Dalton Rushing
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells most of the story: 11.7% and a .342 xwOBA say there's genuine damage when he connects, and a 9.7% walk rate means he'll earn his share of free passes. The problem is a 31.0% whiff rate that ranks in the 16th percentile, and 27.7% strikeouts that bleed directly into the projection's .248/.332/.450 line — the power plays up at catcher, but the contact issues cap how much of it shows up in the box score. If he tightens the swing-and-miss even modestly, the barrel rate and walk rate are enough to profile as a solid regular behind the plate for the Dodgers. If the whiff rate holds where it is, he's a below-average-contact catcher with pop, which in Los Angeles probably still gets him 357 plate appearances and a roster spot, just nothing more.

reports.name: Bubba Chandler

reports.name: Dasan Hill
reports.published_report: The strikeout number is absurd: 15.2 K/9 at A+, 71 punchouts in 42 innings, translating to 9.8 per nine in an MLB context against a league baseline of 8.6. Everything else on this card is a problem. His 7.9 BB/9 at A+ translates to 6.1 at the MLB level, and his 1.8 WHIP reflects what happens when elite swing-and-miss lives alongside a walk rate that severe. The K-BB% sits at 17% and percentiles well within the pool, but only because the strikeout rate is dragging up a walk rate that, left unaddressed, makes the whole profile unworkable. If the command develops, the whiff shape gives him a real role; if it doesn't, he's depth, and the 71 strikeouts become trivia.

reports.name: Brooks Brannon
reports.published_report: The ISO is the whole argument and the whole problem. At .567 slugging and a .298 ISO at AA, Brooks Brannon has legitimate over-the-fence power — 17 home runs in 275 plate appearances is a real thump for a 22-year-old first baseman, and the .921 OPS sits at the 93rd percentile among hitters in the pool. But the translation to an MLB context is where the profile gets complicated: that strikeout rate, already 31% at AA, translates to 30.1% at the MLB level against a backdrop where most big-league hitters strike out well below that, and there is almost no margin for a first baseman who can't put the barrel on the ball against quality arms. If the swing-and-miss tightens up, the power (.194 ISO equivalent) plays at least as a platoon piece; if it doesn't, you're left with a bench corner bat who needs to earn his roster spot every spring. ValuCast has him cooling, down 22 spots in three days.

reports.name: Eliazar Dishmey
reports.published_report: The 3.10 ERA across AA & A+ is the headline, but the walk rate is the one thing standing between a real prospect and a depth arm. Across 73.4 innings, Dishmey has punched out 96 hitters against 38 walks, and when you translate that to an MLB context the strikeout rate clears league average while the 4.5 BB/9 equivalent runs more than a full walk above it — the K-BB% lands right at the MLB mean, which means the strikeout stuff is essentially covering for the command. The WHIP sitting at 1.1 keeps the ERA pretty, but that number has less cushion than it looks like if the walks don't come down as he advances. Either he sharpens the zone and becomes a back-end rotation piece with a real strikeout profile, or the command stays where it is and he's organizational depth.

reports.name: Carmen Mlodzinski
reports.published_report: The 3.46 projection ERA is doing a lot of heavy lifting against a 4.85 xERA, and the Statcast profile explains why the skepticism is warranted. His 18.4% strikeout rate sits in the 23rd percentile, his 21.0% whiff rate in the 20th, and hitters are barreling him at 46.9% hard-hit contact, a 5th-percentile outcome for the pitcher. The walk rate is fine at 7.7% and the fastball sits 95.0 mph, but without swing-and-miss to back the velo, that heater is getting hit hard. If the contact suppression doesn't show up in a full season, what's left is a back-end arm stretched into a starting role with soft strikeout stuff and a hard-hit problem, which is a long-relief profile wearing a rotation jersey.

reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
